latent_mechanisms.display_name: HSV neuroinvasion or latent CNS-reactivation gateway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: HSV-1 reactivation from trigeminal/olfactory-associated latency and HSV-2 primary or recurrent neuroinvasion create the entry state for sporadic herpes simplex encephalitis. This is not all viral encephalitis; it reflects HSV tropism for limbic and frontotemporal brain networks.
Viable HSV replicates in neurons, glia, and local tissue compartments, sustaining viral antigen load, necrotizing inflammation, and PCR-detectable pathogen signal when sampled at the right time.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Limbic, temporal, insular, and orbitofrontal tropism
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: HSV encephalitis preferentially injures medial temporal lobes, hippocampus, amygdala, insula, cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortex, explaining fever plus acute memory, behavior, language, seizure, and focal neurologic syndromes.
HSV causes necrotizing cortical inflammation with endothelial injury, petechial hemorrhage, RBC leakage into CSF, and rare frank temporal lobe hematoma or mass effect.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: CSF and brain innate inflammatory response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Microglial, astrocytic, and recruited leukocyte response to HSV produces fever, headache, meningeal irritation, CSF pleocytosis, elevated CSF protein, and systemic inflammatory markers. Early or immunosuppressed cases can have little or no CSF pleocytosis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Blood-brain barrier disruption, edema, and intracranial pressure pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflamed necrotic cortex and leaky cerebral microvasculature generate vasogenic and cytotoxic edema, mass effect, raised intracranial pressure, vomiting, depressed consciousness, herniation risk, and ICU-level monitoring needs.
Inflamed hippocampal and temporal cortical circuits produce focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, lateralized periodic discharges, and nonconvulsive status epilepticus.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cortical network dysfunction for consciousness, behavior, and language
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Temporal, insular, cingulate, and frontal injury disrupts alertness, orientation, behavior, memory, speech output, comprehension, and focal neurologic function.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Accumulated neuronal injury from delayed effective antiviral exposure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Untreated HSV replication and inflammation rapidly accumulate irreversible limbic/cortical injury; delayed active antiviral exposure raises mortality and long-term cognitive, language, seizure, and focal deficit burden.

After HSV encephalitis, exposed neuronal antigens and immune activation can trigger autoimmune encephalitis, often anti-NMDA receptor mediated, causing relapsing psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias, or encephalopathy despite falling viral burden.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: The gateway event seeds HSV into CNS tissue where local replication drives disease.
HSV replication is concentrated in limbic and frontotemporal tissue in classic disease.
Viral antigen and infected-cell injury activate microglia, cytokines, and CSF leukocyte recruitment.
HSV tropic cortical infection evolves into necrotizing hemorrhagic inflammation in affected tissue.
Necrotic and hemorrhagic cortex disrupts the blood-brain barrier and produces edema and mass effect.
Mesial temporal and insular irritation is highly epileptogenic.
Limbic, cingulate, insular, and temporal cortical involvement directly causes altered mentation and language/behavioral syndromes.
Ongoing viral replication without active antiviral exposure accumulates permanent neuronal injury.
Necrotic HSV-injured tissue can expose neuronal antigens and trigger delayed autoimmune encephalitis.
Cytokine response commonly produces fever, though fever can be absent in elderly or immunosuppressed patients.
Reported fever is a common presenting clue.
Inflamed meninges, edema, and raised pressure produce headache.
Meningeal irritation can produce photophobia.
HSV encephalitis can present with meningoencephalitis and mild-to-moderate meningismus.
HSV meningoencephalitis usually inflames CSF, but normal early CSF occurs.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: can remain normal early or in immunosuppressed hosts
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Typical CSF has lymphocytic pleocytosis, often 10-200 cells/uL, with broader ranges in severe cases.
CSF shifts toward mononuclear/lymphocytic predominance in viral encephalitis.
Barrier disruption and inflammation raise CSF protein, usually modestly.
Hemorrhagic necrosis can leak RBCs into CSF, but absence of RBCs does not exclude HSV encephalitis.
Viable HSV replication in CNS tissue produces PCR-detectable viral nucleic acid in CSF when sampled in the diagnostic window.
HSV PCR positivity is the core pathogen-specific microbiologic evidence for HSV encephalitis and can be positive even when early CSF cell count is normal.
HSV-1 is the common adult encephalitis subtype and pathogen-specific PCR identifies this context.
HSV-2 can cause encephalitis or meningoencephalitis, especially in immunocompromised or atypical adult presentations.
MRI commonly shows limbic and temporal FLAIR/T2/DWI abnormalities.
Medial temporal lobe T2/FLAIR/DWI hyperintensity is the classic imaging signature.
Insular involvement commonly accompanies temporal lobe HSV lesions.
Cingulate extension is part of the HSV limbic pattern in many cases.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: uncommon extension; basal ganglia-predominant disease should raise alternative etiologies
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Thalamic involvement is rare but documented and can occur with otherwise typical temporal HSV disease.
Edematous necrotizing tissue causes swelling, sulcal effacement, and mass effect on imaging.
Frank temporal hemorrhage is rare but mechanistically linked to necrotizing vascular injury.
Focal or generalized seizures are common in HSV encephalitis.
Temporal-limbic HSV can cause nonconvulsive or convulsive status epilepticus.
EEG often shows temporal slowing, lateralized periodic discharges, or epileptiform activity.
Encephalitis of limbic and cortical networks produces confusion, lethargy, delirium, or coma.
Temporal/orbitofrontal involvement can present as agitation, psychosis-like behavior, personality change, or aggression.
Dominant temporal and perisylvian involvement causes dysphasia or aphasia.
Focal weakness, visual field change, cranial deficits, or language deficits reflect focal cortical injury.
Raised ICP and systemic illness commonly cause nausea and vomiting.
Barrier disruption and necrosis raise edema event risk.
Edema, hemorrhage, and mass effect create raised ICP and herniation risk.
Necrotizing vasculitis-like injury can culminate in temporal lobe hemorrhage.
Depressed consciousness, seizures, edema, and ICP threats often require ICU monitoring.
Seizures and impaired airway reflexes increase aspiration risk.
Delayed effective antiviral exposure increases permanent cognitive, language, memory, and seizure sequelae.
Delayed post-HSV autoimmune relapse is an outcome-relevant complication distinct from ongoing viral replication.
Untreated or late-treated HSV encephalitis has high mortality; accumulated irreversible CNS injury and complications drive death risk.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Inflammatory CSF pleocytosis and barrier leak tend to raise protein together, except in early normocellular cases.
HSV CSF often becomes lymphocyte-predominant after the earliest phase.
Recurrent focal or generalized seizures can transition into convulsive or nonconvulsive status epilepticus.
Status epilepticus often requires airway protection, deep sedation, and ventilation.
Seizure and impaired airway reflexes increase aspiration risk.
Imaging mass effect is a direct marker of raised ICP risk.
Temporal hematoma can cause mass effect, midline shift, and herniation physiology.
Large hemorrhage and lobectomy/decompression increase risk of persistent deficits despite survival.
Raised ICP and herniation physiology are major short-term death pathways.
Refractory seizures and ventilation-associated complications raise short-term mortality.
Acyclovir crystal nephropathy is a direct treatment-to-AKI pathway.
AKI clinically manifests through rising creatinine and dosing constraints.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Thymidine-kinase-deficient or polymerase-mutant HSV can substantially reduce acyclovir activity, especially in immunocompromised hosts with prior antiviral exposure.
Renal dose adjustment is needed; under-adjustment increases nephrotoxicity while over-reduction can lower CNS antiviral exposure.
Poor hydration and rapid infusion increase acyclovir crystalluria and AKI risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Crystal nephropathy risk rises with renal impairment, dehydration, rapid infusion, and high dose exposure.
Creatinine rise can constrain dosing and antiviral exposure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Core HSV-directed antiviral vector field for suspected or confirmed HSV encephalitis; active exposure changes viral replication before downstream edema and neuronal injury resolve.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Foscarnet bypasses HSV thymidine kinase activation and remains active against many acyclovir-resistant strains.
Foscarnet is nephrotoxic and requires close renal and electrolyte monitoring.

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity is clinically important and may limit antiviral exposure.
Electrolyte derangements can lower seizure threshold.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative HSV-directed vector when acyclovir activity or tolerability is inadequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit depends on clinical or electrographic seizure activity rather than HSV replication itself.
Renal adjustment is needed for levetiracetam exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: Deep sedation for refractory seizures can require airway support.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls seizure-driven injury and aspiration/ventilation hazards while antiviral therapy reshapes HSV replication.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Osmotic therapy affects ICP and edema physiology, not HSV replication.
Mannitol can worsen renal stress; sodium/osmolality monitoring constrains hypertonic saline.

side_effects.interpretation: Mannitol and osmotic stress can worsen kidney risk in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporizes edema and ICP while definitive antiviral and neurosurgical decisions proceed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large temporal hematoma with midline shift is a decompression pathway.
Benefit is through pressure relief and herniation prevention.

side_effects.interpretation: Neurosurgical intervention carries procedure-related bleeding risk.
Large lesions requiring surgery already carry high residual deficit risk; procedure can add focal deficit risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Pressure-relief vector for large hemorrhage, refractory edema, hydrocephalus, or impending herniation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Organ support is activated by airway, oxygenation, coma, or seizure physiology.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedation can worsen or mask apparent encephalopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports oxygenation and airway safety during coma, status epilepticus, aspiration, or ICP-directed sedation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: The protective value is larger when baseline renal reserve is poor.

treatments.context_specific_role: Keeps active antiviral exposure feasible by reducing nephrotoxicity and preserving doseable renal clearance.

neonate.trajectory_modulation: Neonatal HSV CNS disease more often follows disseminated or peripartum infection and may have diffuse or multifocal imaging rather than classic adult temporal-only disease.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Neonatal disease can be more diffuse.
Neonatal CNS or disseminated HSV has high mortality and neurodevelopmental sequelae risk.

older_adult.trajectory_modulation: Older adults have higher encephalitis severity, more muted fever in some cases, and worse recovery reserve.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Lower cognitive reserve can make encephalopathy more prominent.
Age worsens critical illness and neurologic outcome.

steroids_transplant_malignancy_hiv_or_bi.trajectory_modulation: Raises reactivation risk, can blunt fever/CSF pleocytosis, and increases concern for acyclovir-resistant HSV after prolonged antiviral exposure.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Immunosuppressed patients may have less CSF cellular response.
Fever can be muted by host immune suppression or steroids.
Resistance is concentrated in immunocompromised patients with prior antiviral selection.

tlr3_pathway_or_related_inborn_error.trajectory_modulation: Childhood or recurrent HSV encephalitis can reflect impaired interferon pathway sensing in CNS-resident cells.

brain_radiation_neurosurgery_tumor_or_ol.trajectory_modulation: Local CNS injury may create diagnostic confusion and may reduce reserve against edema, seizures, or hemorrhage.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pre-existing cortical injury lowers seizure threshold.

delay_after_neurologic_symptom_onset.trajectory_modulation: Does not cause HSV encephalitis but allows viral replication, necrotizing inflammation, and accumulated treatment-delay injury to rise.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Longer viral injury raises residual deficit risk.
Untreated disease has substantially higher mortality.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not raise HSV prior but changes acyclovir dose, toxicity, and probability of treatment interruption.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Poor renal clearance and dehydration raise crystal nephropathy risk.
Renal dosing errors or treatment interruption can lower antiviral coverage.

maternal_primary_or_active_genital_hsv_n.trajectory_modulation: Raises neonatal HSV CNS disease risk and changes prevention and neonatal evaluation context.

pregnant_adult.trajectory_modulation: Adult HSV encephalitis can occur in pregnancy; fetal/maternal safety and renal volume status constrain treatment monitoring more than disease geometry.

supportive_care: Treat HSV encephalitis as a time-sensitive neurologic emergency: do not wait for confirmatory HSV PCR when fever plus encephalopathy, seizure, focal deficit, or temporal-limbic MRI/EEG features make HSV plausible.

Keep CSF HSV PCR, brain biopsy, and pathogen confirmation as confirmatory/context evidence; presentation ranking should rely on fever, headache, mental status, seizures, focal deficits, CSF inflammation, MRI, EEG, vitals, and course.
Lumbar puncture when safe: record opening pressure, CSF WBC and differential, RBC count, protein, glucose, bacterial studies, HSV-1/2 PCR, VZV/enterovirus testing, and paired serum glucose.
Brain MRI with DWI/ADC, FLAIR, T2, GRE/SWI, and contrast when feasible; CT can be normal early and is mainly used for safety, hemorrhage, and mass-effect assessment.
Continuous or repeated EEG for obtunded patients, unexplained fluctuating mental status, subtle automatisms, or suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus.
ICU-level monitoring for depressed consciousness, recurrent seizures, status epilepticus, focal deficits, mass effect, hemorrhage, need for airway protection, or rapidly worsening edema.

Monitor and prevent acyclovir toxicity: check baseline and daily creatinine during acute therapy, maintain adequate IV hydration, avoid rapid infusion, adjust dose to renal function, and avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins.
Track neurologic exam serially: orientation, language, memory, cranial nerves, motor asymmetry, visual fields, seizure recurrence, and Glasgow Coma Scale or similar structured consciousness score.

Manage ICP physiology with head elevation, normoxia, normocapnia, fever control, sodium/osmolality monitoring, osmotic therapy when needed, and neurosurgical input for hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or refractory mass effect.
Airway and aspiration prevention: swallow precautions, early airway protection when GCS or seizure burden threatens airway reflexes, and surveillance for aspiration pneumonia.

After acute HSV encephalitis, monitor for relapsing psychiatric symptoms, dyskinesias, seizures, or encephalopathy suggesting post-HSV autoimmune encephalitis rather than persistent viral replication alone.

Rehabilitation planning for survivors: cognitive therapy, speech/language therapy, seizure follow-up, neuropsychological assessment, driving restrictions where relevant, and family education about relapse or seizure warning signs.
